name: Chandramouleeswarar Temple, Thiruvakkarai
deity: Shiva as Chandramouleeswarar (Piraisoodiya Emperuman), with the goddess Vadivambikai (Amirthambikai)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Thondai country, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); structural temple raised in stone by the Cholas (10th century) with later additions
dynasty: Cholas (with the endowments of queen Sembiyan Mahadevi)
summary: Chandramouleeswarar at Thiruvakkarai is the Tevaram shrine the hymns call Tiruvakkarai, an ancient Shiva temple on the bank of the Varaha river below a low hill, famed alike for its fierce guardian goddess Vakrakali and for the forest of petrified wood that lies turned to stone beside the town.

sections.history: Thiruvakkarai stands in the old Thondai country, in what is now Villupuram district, a short way inland from the coast near Puducherry and Auroville. In the Tevaram hymns the town is called Tiruvakkarai, and because its Lord was praised in song by the Nayanmar saints it is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams of the Thondai region. The name is traced to the older word Vakkarai, and tradition ties it to the asura Vakra whose story the place still keeps. Though the shrine is far older in veneration, the temple that stands today was raised in stone during the Chola age, around the tenth century, and is remembered as having received the gracious endowments of the Chola queen Sembiyan Mahadevi. It has been kept in continuous worship since, a very old sanctuary beside a river and a hill.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a seven-tiered rajagopuram and sits at the foot of a low hill on the bank of the river the hymns call the Varaha. Within the enclosure the sanctum of Chandramouleeswarar holds the Shiva linga, the Lord named for the crescent moon he bears upon his crest, honoured also as Piraisoodiya Emperuman. The goddess Vadivambikai, worshipped too as Amirthambikai, abides in her own shrine, while the fierce guardian goddess Vakrakali is enshrined in the form for which the town is widely known. Carved in the Dravidian manner, the stone walls carry inscriptions of the temple's medieval patrons, and the pillared halls and the river setting lend the place the gravity of great age.
sections.legends: The defining story of Thiruvakkarai belongs to the asura Vakra, the demon from whom the town is said to take its name. In the local telling Vakra was a being of fearsome power whom the gods could not subdue, and the land was delivered only when the demon was slain here, the river that runs below the temple keeping in its name the memory of that deliverance. The goddess enshrined as Vakrakali is honoured as the fierce mother who ended the demon and guarded the helpless in the moment of her victory, and to this day the priests cover her image in sandalwood paste at the new moon. Woven through these accounts is the older grace of Shiva as Chandramouleeswarar, before whom even the dreadful was turned to peace. Some details of the legend vary from one source to another, as is natural for a story carried so long by memory.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps its daily round of worship and a cycle of yearly festivals through the Tamil months. Chithirai brings the Chitra Pournami festival on the full moon, and Maha Shivaratri is observed with night-long vigil as at every Shiva temple. Vinayaka Chaturthi, Vijayadasami, and Karthigai Deepam are kept in their seasons, and the goddess Vakrakali is specially honoured at each new moon, when her image is anointed with sandalwood. The temple draws particular crowds on new moon days; confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Thiruvakkarai rewards a visit made without haste. Enter beneath the eastern gopuram, come first to the sanctum of Chandramouleeswarar, then to the goddess Vadivambikai in her own shrine, and do not leave without the darshan of the fierce Vakrakali for whom many make the journey. The river below the temple and the low hill behind it keep the setting quiet, a world apart from the coastal road. Many travellers pair the temple with the National Fossil Wood Park beside the town, where trees twenty million years old lie turned wholly to stone, so that a day here holds both the living sanctuary and the forest that time itself has made unchanging.

visit.timings: Commonly open in the morning from around 6 a.m. until early afternoon and again from late afternoon into the evening, with the temple often open through the full day at the new moon; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruvakkarai lies in Vanur taluk of Villupuram district, about 30 km from Tindivanam and roughly 29 km from Villupuram, and is easily reached from Puducherry near Auroville. Buses and taxis serve the village, and the temple stands at its heart, close to the National Fossil Wood Park.
